title: The Bat and the Weasels
attribution: Excerpted verbatim from Aesop's Fables, translated by V. S. Vernon Jones (1912), via Project Gutenberg.
body: A Bat fell to the ground and was caught by a Weasel, and was just going to be killed and eaten when it begged to be let go. The Weasel said he couldn't do that because he was an enemy of all birds on principle. "Oh, but," said the Bat, "I'm not a bird at all: I'm a mouse." "So you are," said the Weasel, "now I come to look at you"; and he let it go. Some time after this the Bat was caught in just the same way by another Weasel, and, as before, begged for its life. "No," said the Weasel, "I never let a mouse go by any chance." "But I'm not a mouse," said the Bat; "I'm a bird." "Why, so you are," said the Weasel; and he too let the Bat go.
Look and see which way the wind blows before you commit yourself.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what happens to the Bat right at the start?
options: He is chased out of his cave by an owl
He is trapped in a hunter's net
He falls to the ground and is caught by a Weasel
He collides with a tree branch at night

questions.prompt: According to the passage, why does the first Weasel say he must kill the Bat?
options: He is an enemy of all birds on principle
He is very hungry and needs food
He was ordered to by another animal
He caught the Bat stealing from him

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Bat claim to be when caught by the first Weasel?
options: A bird
A small owl
A moth
A mouse

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the second Weasel say he never does?
options: Let a bird go by any chance
Let a mouse go by any chance
Hunt after the sun has set
Share his catch with another weasel

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Bat claim to be when caught by the second Weasel?
options: A mouse
A butterfly
A bird
A small snake

questions.prompt: According to the passage, how do both encounters end for the Bat?
options: He is let go both times
He is eaten by the second Weasel
He escapes without speaking either time
He is kept as a pet by both Weasels

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does the Bat claim to be a different creature each time he is caught?
options: He genuinely forgets what kind of creature he is
He wants to trick the Weasels into fighting each other
He believes both Weasels are actually the same animal
He notices what each Weasel refuses to harm and claims to be that instead

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, what does the Bat's success both times reveal about his approach to danger?
options: Physical strength ultimately saves him from both Weasels
Adapting his claim to fit each captor's stated enemy keeps him safe
Speed alone allows him to slip away unnoticed
Loyalty to his true identity wins him mercy

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does it mean that the Weasel was an enemy of birds "on principle"?
options: Only when a bird had personally wronged him
As a joke rather than something he truly believed
As a firm rule he holds, not because of anything one bird did
Because a law required him to act that way

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the point of the fable, given its closing line?
options: Reading the situation and adapting to it can help you survive danger
Telling the truth is always the safest course of action
Weasels are more easily fooled than most other animals
Bats should avoid the ground at all costs

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Bat do the moment he is about to be killed?
options: He bites the Weasel to escape
He pretends to already be dead
He offers the Weasel food instead
He begs to be let go

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the first Weasel say once the Bat claims to be a mouse?
options: "I don't believe you," and refuses
"So you are," and lets him go
"Prove it," and demands evidence
"It makes no difference," and attacks anyway

questions.prompt: According to the passage, when is the Bat caught by the second Weasel?
options: The very next morning
While he was still speaking to the first Weasel
Some time after the first encounter
Many years after the first encounter

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why doesn't the Bat repeat his first claim of being a mouse to the second Weasel?
options: This Weasel has said he never lets a mouse go, so that claim would fail
He has forgotten that claim worked before
The second Weasel already knows he is a bat
He prefers to be honest with the second Weasel

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, what do the two Weasels have in common despite reaching opposite decisions?
options: Each one is easily distracted from finishing the job
Each one is more forgiving than most weasels
Each one secretly wants to keep the Bat as a pet
Each one refuses to harm a creature it does not consider its enemy

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does it mean to "commit yourself" in the closing line?
options: To promise something to a stranger
To settle firmly on one choice or side
To admit a mistake openly
To ask for someone else's opinion first

questions.prompt: Which of these best summarizes what happens in the passage?
options: A Bat is caught once and never escapes again
Two Weasels argue over which of them may eat the Bat
A Bat twice talks his way free by claiming to be whatever each captor won't harm
A Bat convinces two Weasels to become friends
